OK, we should be in that area now. Interview today with Sam Jones. Sam, I think probably the best thing for us to start out with is--maybe why don't you just give like a brief background, you know, on yourself in terms of how--you know, where you're from, how you began to start playing music, how you became interested in music and just really started getting involved.

OK. Well, I was born in Jacksonville, Florida, November 12th, 1924. As a--as a child, you know, most families, black families from the South, everybody would have a piano in their house. Uh, everybody that I've came in contact with had a--had a member of the family that played in the choir at the church so there was music around the house. And I had an uncle that played a guitar. On the weekends when everybody would get together, you know, whiskey was too expensive so they'd drink moonshine, what they call moonshine, see.
Yeah.
Drink it out of cups and stuff. So, every--you know how everybody get together, you know, sit around and you start playing the blues and stuff on the guitar.
Uh huh.
And naturally that's the melodies and stuff from the blues and the--and the--and the sound and the chords and things coming from the guitar fascinated

me and I sit there and watch. And uh, but as I grew, my family moved from Jacksonville to Tampa, Florida. That's where I attended school there--elementary school, junior high, high school. So uh, when I got to be in junior high school--by the time I got to junior high school I was a pretty good guitar player. And during that--at that time, you know, because I had just picked it up by ear by listening at my uncle, you know. And so I could sit down and rip off some blues and stuff, you know--
Uh huh.
And sing along with it--the blues that he--I heard around the house, you know.
Uh huh.
And uh, one thing led to another then I become--people began to have me come in the church on programs and stuff and have--have me play on programs in the church and stuff.
Uh huh.
And then sing, you know. That ended when uh, they had me to come to play for a funeral one time. And so that ended my--
Really?
My church stuff, you know.
How old were you during that time?
I was about 13, I think.
Thirteen?
Thirteen or 14.
Uh huh.

But before that time, I had a--I was always sort of a sickly type fellow. I was born with a affective infected kidney. And I stayed in the hospital for a long time--almost a year and a half--because of the--now, you know, what they--they wasn't up on the medicine that they are today. Where today, that they can give you a pill which can flush your kidneys, clean all the flames and stuff around your kidneys. And you're fine. You know what I mean?
Uh huh.
But uh, at that time they had to operate and put a tube into my side, you know.
Hmm.
And therefore, to drain with a jug on the floor with a thing running from my side into this jug which was--would drain all this pus and stuff from around my kidneys.
Uh huh.

So, I got to be better and after that, I sort of--after that was over with. And now--I was walking down the street in Tampa one day--you know, the main drag--I was, I don't know, I was going on an errand for my family one day, you know. And uh, you know, in Florida, everything is open down there--you know the bars, you know, all the doors and everything was wide open. And so, you know, most

every place had the juke boxes, you know the--sitting in the, you know, sitting in the door. They never would have them sitting in the back. They all--they would always be sitting in the door, you know.
Uh huh.
And I was walking down the street and I heard a--a record playing. And it was a--I don't know if you remember a blues singer named Wynonie Harris?
Oh yeah.
OK, well it was Wynonie Harris used to uh, do most of his recordings with jazz musicians. All of his--if you'll notice on all of his recordings, he did it with jazz musicians--with Oscar Pettiford --
Uh huh.
Big Sid Catlett ... all those guys on the drums.
Uh huh.

And this Oscar Pettiford had a 12-bar solo, had one close in his blues. And I heard that shit and I said--and I think I had a dime in my pocket--but during that time it cost a nickle to play. And I went back to the juke box and I asked the man what song was that. And he told me. And he--I told him could I hear that--could I hear that--that record again. So he said yeah, you know. So I gave him my dime and he gave me a nickle back. And I put a nickle on that--on that thing. And it played it again. And it was a bass solo on there,
but it sounds like a saxophone, you know.
Hmm.
And I was--I was fascinated by it. I didn't know exactly what that bass was, you know. All I knew, I liked what I heard.
Yeah.
And I took my other nickle and put it back there too. And so--and that was my car fare home. So I had to walk home from across town.
Yeah.
See I lived in a part of the city called Ybor City, which was a Spanish neighborhood.
Uh huh.
Cubans and the Italians--that's where I came up at.
Uh huh.

So I was way across town and, you know, and so I said, well--I walked home then. And I--I kept that in mind, man. And at that time we had a--my teacher, my science teacher who's an alto saxophone player. He played in--at night. And he would come to work in class, man, and he would--he was a very good teacher but he would take nods, you know, between, you know, uh, speeches and stuff, you know. He could tell you what's happening, you know, he'd give you your assignment, what to do, but I used to watch him going to sleep, you know, cause he worked late
at night. And also the--Mr. Rodriguez, our band master, he also played at night. He worked, he worked at a night club.
Uh huh.

So--but I--and so he had a--put a--he put a band together, like a 16 piece, you know, dance band, from the school. And also, I was still playing guitar in the band, so we didn't have a bass in the band.
Uh huh.
So I went on and conned my--my folks to loan me some bread. And I saw a bass downtown and--that I wanted. And it was a pretty reasonable, you know.
Uh huh.
So, I don't how, you know, it came out. It worked out alright. They agreed so we went downtown and they let me have the bass on, on time, you know, I'd make payments on it.
Uh huh.

On account of my old--you know, my old man was working--working for the city water department. And so that was cool. And stupid me, I went and took a-- I don't know if you've heard of this story or not. I did this--they wrote about this in the Downbeat Magazine quite a few years ago. I took the bass. You know, I thought it was hip to paint the bass white, you know.
Yeah.
Because all the pictures you see, you know, have the guys playing bass, basses would be white, you know.
Uh huh.
Blonde.
Blonde, yeah.

So I took some house paint--and this was a hell of a bass, man, really this was one of the--hell of a--bass had a hell of a sound. Had to be old, you know. I'm a kid. I'm still a teenager, you know. And I took some house paint and painted the damn bass. And that was the end of that bass. That fucked the bass all up, man. The bass didn't have no sound. But, but anyway, several of the little jive bands around town--there was a band called--a band leader round there, a guy who had a bunch of young guys. And they called him Clarinet Brown. He was teaching stock, you know, to the kids. And he was playing all that, you know, that stock music.
Oh yeah.
Count Basie stock and Harry James and Benny Goodman and all that shit.
Right.

Count Basie's and--and then one thing led to another. There was a--there was a quintet playing in a club right on the corner of Central and Scott. And uh, I guess these people saw me carrying this bass and they--
and these was like old men. These were men--all of them was in their 40's and 50's, you know.
Uh huh.
They didn't have a bass player in there, you know. And this place--if I can remember the name--sit right on the corner. It was a bar in front and a club in back of the bar, you know.
Uh huh.
Well anyway, these men had approached me and asked me did I want to play--did I wanted the job.
Uh huh.

To play with them. I said man, 'you're kidding me. Yes, sir', you know I told them. So he say, and so they work four nights a week. They work from uh, yeah Wednesday--Wednesday, Thursday, Friday and Saturday they worked. So I told them yes sir. And I--and I worked the first week and when they paid me off, they gave--they gave the, you know these little envelopes, little brown envelopes.
Uh huh.

So he gave me my money. And the guy was passing out the money to everybody, you know. And so I didn't know exactly how much money--I didn't care because I was just having a ball, myself, you know. And some of those bad notes worked, you know. You know, I didn't know
what the hell I was doing, you know.
Yeah.
But sometime when you luck up on a good note--
Uh huh.
Sometime and uh--but I was all--I was ...by me being familiar with the guitar--with the first-- the top four strings. It made it a little easier for me, you know.
Uh huh.
Especially if they play the blues, now, you see. If they play the blues, I was right in there, you know.
Yeah.

When they start playing standards and them old standards and stuff, then I--they lost me a little bit. But sometime I would luck up on--like I said, luck up on a good note and it would sound alright. So I took the money out of the envelope and there was $50 in there. Fifty fucking dollars, man. I ain't never seen $50 in my life, you know. And I told them--asked the man "did you give me too much money?" And he said, "what do you mean, give you too much money. You want more?" You know, I said, "no,sir." And he said, "well, take the money. That's your pay, you know." And I ran, man. I ran from Central Avenue to Ybor City. I mean that's way across town, man.
Uh huh.

I ran home and showed my--woke them up. They was sleeping. Went in there and showed. And I made more--I made more money than my--than my uncle made, man. Working for the city. He didn't make but $40 a week.
Uh huh. Uh huh.
I brought home $50, man and I ain't worked but four days, you see.
Uh huh.

And they woke up and say, 'you mean to tell me this is what you got for playing the bass?' I say, 'yes sir.' And everybody was amazed. I mean, I was so--and so that wiped everything else out. You see, well this is it. I'm not doing nothing but playing bass. This is it. If I can make $50 for playing four days, man. And my uncle out there in sun working eight hours a day for--coming in--his pay coming in like forty-some dollars, man, after they take out, you know.
Yeah, right.

So, one thing led on to another, and then I--the Brass Rail. I started meeting guys, ....younger musician. And there was another grown man. His name was Ralph Dewey. So he got me to play the bass and another friend of mine to play the drums and a saxophone player named Johnny Burdine. All of us was young. We was, you
know, in the same age. And working at a club downtown Tampa called the Brass Rail.
Mmmmm.

Making $125 a week, you see. And we stayed down there, man, for about two or three years. And I had--I was learning more and more about the bass. Then I was pretty much up on it, then at that time. Then there was a lot of animosity around town because there I am, a teenager, making $125 a week. I owned an automobile. I bought myself a car. I'd wear suits, you know.
Uh huh.

And I got my girls and stuff and the guys in town, they don't like this, see. They don't like for a guy to, you know what I mean. We three guys, you know, ordinarily, we--when we walked--would walk in a dance, you know, cause we get off around--we be through around 12:30, 1:00 o'clock down there. And so we go to a nightclub, you know, come--and the guys would like to, you know, jump on you, you know, fight you, you know. Because the girls, you know, they see us coming and they say, 'oh, there's the magnificent three,' you know. Well, and so we decided to move from our--then I got another job in the best band in town called the Honey Dippers.
Uh hmm.
Not the Honey Drippers, the Honey Dippers.
The Honey Dippers, uh huh.
Yeah, this man was Charlie Brantley.
Uh huh.

He had the best band in town. Now this is where my association with Ray Charles come. See, Ray Charles was the piano player in this band. And if you will remember the popular music at that time was uh, Charles Brown in the pop field and Louis Jordan in the pop field. OK, well this band played all their music, man.
Uh huh.
Especially with Louis Jordan. We had-- the band, this band had the identity. See, this guy would copy the identical arrangement from the record.
Uh huh.
You see. And he had a vocalist named Clarence Jolly who sang all of Louis Jordan's songs. And he had the exact arrangements, you know.
Uh huh.
Of Louis Jordan's Tympany Five.
Uh huh.
Ray Charles would sing all the Charles Brown and Nat Cole songs at the piano.
Uh huh.
And you know, he would do that part of it, you know.
Uh huh.
So that way, we worked seven nights a week, every week. Never was off, man. We used to pray for a day off, you know.
Uh huh.

Because we played all the proms all over the state of Florida and all of the club dances--all of the affairs, man. We was the band that played. And it was a--like a--it was a four horn line. You know, we had a trombone, trumpet, two saxophones, guitar, bass, drums and piano.
Uh huh.
So, what is that--eight pieces? It was about eight pieces. Yeah, say about eight. Yeah. And Ray Charles was the piano player.

Yeah? Well, the two of you must have really gotten close, huh, during that time. Because I was just--a little slight digression from, not to cut you off--but I noticed I read his book. And he mentions about like when he came to Tampa and he spoke a lot about you. And, you know, how tight the two of you got. Have you read the book?
No.
Yeah. He talks about you in the book--about when you came--
And so, uh--
He gets into some wild stuff. It's a wild
book. I have not met him personally.
Yeah, he was a wild--
He sound like a wild cat.

He was the wild man when he was a kid, man. He was blind, too, and he was still wild. And he was something, man. And he said well, you know, we are-- well, we'd liked him so much because he wasn't in a handicapped blind dude, man.
Uh huh.

He did everything himself. He came to work by himself. You'd tell him where to meet and he'd be there, man. He could--you'd see him coming down the streets feeling his way and he'd get there, you know.
Uh huh.
Never would see nobody walking with him, leading him anyplace. He did everything by himself.
Uh huh.

You know. And uh--well, we got a lot of girls from, from his stuff, you know. Had a hell of a reputation. And so he decide to get a trio. Cause, like I said, did that Charles Brown stuff. You remember that?
Yeah.
Blazes with Charles Brown. And he sang all them songs, man. And so me and the guitar player--his name--we used to call him Box--started a trio around there, around, around Florida.
Uh huh.
So he got an offer to go to, to leave Tampa and go to Seattle, Washington to play out there in a club. So I said no, I'd better--I'd better stay around home here, you know what I mean.
Uh huh.

I ain't never been, you know, that far, you know what I mean. And I don't want to go out there and take no chances. And, sure enough, another guitar player went with him named Gossett E. McKey. And they went out there and sure enough he went out there and got hooked on some drugs and stuff.
Ohhh.
Out there.
Uh huh.

So I stayed home and I continued playing with the Charley Brantley's band. So we got another piano player from--a boy came from Detroit. And so I--we played with that band until we got tired of that. And Johnny Burdine and myself, we decided to move on down to Miami, you know. Big time lifetime stuff--you know, the New York and the Florida, you know. So we moved on down there to Miami. We had a job down there working with another constituent of ours from Tampa. His name was Reuben Phillips. Reuben Phillips, not Reuben, Rubin Phillipps, but Rubin Mitchell. Piano player. You see, and when he was in Tampa, he was--

this boy was--he worked in the, he worked in the funeral home, you know. So he got tired of doing that. So we all went down there and we got a job working in a night club called The Entertainers Club. You know, it was like a horseshoe bar.
Uh huh.
And we stayed there. And we worked there a long time. But in, but in the night club room was a band back there named Frank Brown. You ever heard of Frank Brown?
Hmmm. Yeah, I remember the name--Frank Brown.
Frank Brown. Frank Brown used to--used to be up here years ago and he used to write for Buddy Johnson Band, Erskine Hawkins Band and a hell of a big band arranger.
Yeah.
He played trumpet. He had a band. He had a--like a 13-piece band back then in the club.
But Sam, when you were--you said you were-- that you were playing with this, with Charley Brantley's band.
Right.
In, in--that's all while you were still in high school?
No, we--I was out--
But you was out of high school, then.
Yeah.
But you did start playing with--that first incident you were talking about like where you--
Yeah.
You were still in high school.
Right. Yeah.
Yeah.
You know, like to make a long story short, one thing lead into another, you know what I mean.
Uh huh.

And I moved on. And so that's when I--we really got to meet a lot of musicians. I met a lot of musicians in Tampa because when those big bands and things used to come to Tampa, I always met the bus in front of the hotel, you know. And the guys--them guys said "there he is again, waiting for us."
Yeah.

You know, they would always--but I was--I was fascinated about, Jimmie Lunceford's band. For some reason, they kept me--and every one of those guys was gentlemans, man. They would step off the bus like they just came from downtown somewhere. They all had suits on, you know.
Uh huh.
Briefcases with their horns and stuff, man.
Uh huh.

They stepped off that bus, man, say "God Damn," you know. I see other bands step off the bus look like they been through hell, man. Like the Lucky Millinder Band--those guys, they come off--step off the bus. Boy, their hair and shit's standing all up. And that's the first time I saw "Bullmoose"Jackson. But the band that really knocked me out, man--that I--the band that really, really, really knocked me out was Cootie Williams' big band.
Hmm.

Lot of people don't--is not hip to the Cootie Williams big band. Especially younger--the last three or four generations. But in my time, when I was coming up, and I don't think I have heard anything like that yet, except the Bill Eckstine band was close to it. You ever heard the Cootie Williams big band?
I heard some recordings of that. Was this done with--was Bud playing with them?
Bud Powell was playing with them.
When you heard them?
Yeah.
Yeah.
/ "Cleanhead" Eddie Vinson was playing alto.
Uh huh.
And singing. And singing the blues in the band.
Uh huh.

But man, that was one of the helluvist bands I ever heard in my life, man. And I followed that band almost all over the state of Florida, man, in my car. In fact, I had some of the musicians ride in my car, you know.
Oh yeah?
Followed the bus, you know.
Yeah.
Because I never could get enough--never could get enough hearing this band cause their theme song was 'Round Midnight'...And to see 18 dudes stand up--
Uh huh.
And play 'Round Midnight', man. All voiced.
Yeah.

Sort of make your, your flesh crawl to hear that, man. But they had a different channel, now. See, they--they had a different channel* See, Cootie Williams wrote--you know, Cootie Williams and uh, and uh, Thelonious (Monk) wrote 'Round Midnight.'
Hmm. Uh huh.
You see.
So Cootie did write--he did collaborate with--
Yeah.
*'Channel' is musician's jargon for the 'B' (bridge) section of a tune that follows an A-A-B-A structure.
Theloniüs on that.
Yeah.
OK.
Yeah, see now, Cootie--Cootie wrote the channel to "'Bund Midnight." But it was a different--it's a different channel.
Uh huh.
You see.
OK.

Yeah. And the baritone player in that band took sick. I mean he was really sick on night and I took him to the doctor. Woke the doctor up about three o'clock in the morning, man, after he had finished playing.
Uh huh.
And I understand when the band got back to New York, he died.
Hmm.

The baritone player in that band. He was a tall, tall brown-skinned and handsome dude, man. When he's seated down in the orchestra, man, he's smiling, man, he didn't let people know that he was sick, you know.
Hmm.
Played his ass off.
Uh huh.
He was seriously ill and he died.
Uh huh.
When the band got back to New York. And like I said, that was the first time I saw Bud Powell.
Oh, yeah.

And who else was in that band--"Cleanhead" Vinson --had that "Cleanhead" Vinson . That's how he got famous. That's how his name got to be famous because he was the lead soloist in the band. He, I mean he was a hell of a soloist, man. He--you know, he had heard Bird out in Kansas City.
Uh huh.
And he was playing alto. And man, I mean he was playing, playing, too, man. And they had all these arrangements around him, man. And they was--and I mean they was hip. They be jiving.
Yeah.

They would be hip. And I forgot who was in the rhythm section, playing bass in that band.* But anyway, we was working in--in a club, The Entertainers, down there. And they built another club around the corner from us. And I guess it was some big time business men, you know. But the colored didn't last long because they started off with a band. We started off with a--Louis Armstrong orchestra, then went into. They had a big orchestra, right?
Uh huh.
And that's when I met..... --uh, and you know what I'm trying to say--the bass player----Arvell Shaw.
*Possibly Norman Keenan.
Oh, Arvell .
Uh huh. Arvell broke his string. And then came around to my club and ask me for a string. And I'd go reach down in my bag and gave him a string, you know.
Uh huh.
And I used to go around there listening at the Louis Armstrong band between sets, you know.
Oh, so Arvell was playing--he played with the big group, too, huh?
Yeah.
Uh huh.
Arvell was young--he was young, too, man. He was younger, you know.
Yeah.
And he wasn't big and funny looking like-- you know, he was a young dude. And I said--they had a lot of fantastic musicians, man in Miami, you know. In Miami there are a lot of nightclubs.
Hmm.
Lot in there. And all these nightclubs had music in them. We'd play the Rocket Palace--13 piece band in there because he had floor shows, see? They had floor shows in all these clubs.
Uh huh.
And the small bands that plays outside in
the lounge.
Uh huh.
You know.

Well, let me ask you--interject something. Now, in terms of like the racial situation that was happening down there then, how--primarily, I mean, everything that you talked about occured within the black neighborhoods, and was in the black community.
Right. OK.
Yeah. Cause I was trying to get a little parallel in there. I didn't--
Alright. So after we left The Entertainers club--we got fired, incidentally, from The Entertainers club.
Uh huh.
We decided to go back to Tampa to a football game--maroon and gold. That--I say maroon and gold--that's a football game, you know, like a big, big every year, you know.
Uh huh.
And so we decided to go back to Tampa. And we didn't tell the man that we were going. We just got somebody and put another band to play in our place.
Uh huh.
And the band was tired. And this band--and so we came back, the man fired us, you see. Ohhh, you don't have a job here no more. So, so we got fired from that, it's
OK. Now, there was a club called the Harlem Square.
Uh huh.

So I went down to the Harlem Square and hit on the man for a job. This guy was a Jew. His name was Joe--a little 'old short dude. Of course all Jews own--own the nightclubs down there. Really, actually. But his brother was the head of the liquor board, the State of Florida. So, let me make a long story short, the guy gave us--he say, well, I'll give you all a try, if you're, you know, if you're anything, you know--if you all make a, draw a crowd, make some people come in here and come in the lounge. Say, I'll give you all some more--I'll give you some more money, you know. If we make more money, you make more money. So, we don't have nothing to do--nothing to lose. So, so we all--five of us, man--but actually it was six of us--me; Mitchell Robinson, the drummer; Noel Cruz, the piano player, he was a fantastic piano player; and the drummer was....like, man--I ain't heard nobody yet like him; Blue Mitchell; Johnny Burdine, we was still together--me and this saxophone player, Johnny Burdine; and a trombone player named Abe Meeks--Abe Meeks. Our only repertory was nothing but be-bop.
Uh huh.
So we play--we playing all the music we heard. We learn how to play from the records--all the Charlie Parker, all the Dizzy Gillespie's, all the Dexter
Gordon--anything you'd name. Lester--Johnny Burdine, he was a Lester Young man, you know.
Uh huh.
So Abe Meeks, he got drafted in the Army. So that left the five of us. So, now we're really into very dizzying stuff, now.
Uh huh.

OK, so word spread--man, there's five dudes over there at the Harlem Square playing--playing uh, be-bop music. Well, it spreads all over to--all over in Miami Beach. Now the white musicians was coming over here.
Hmm.

And then, they conversing over there, man, and the place is getting packed, jam packed with people, now. And all of a sudden, we're getting a white audience over there. Now, the white people started coming over on Second Avenue in the black town.
Uh huh.
And this shit ain't going to do. And now, they start writing about the shit in the newspaper--about the immigration, the mixing of the races.
Oh yeah.
At the Harlem Square club.
Uh huh.
Chief of Police came over there and said "bullshit. Ya'll get your ass and put 'em out of there, man."
Walked in there and put all them white--made all them white people go back to Miami Beach, wherever you come from.
Oh yeah?
Ran their ass out of there. And so they had a--they booked Sarah Vaughn at the Harlem Square. She had Jimmy Jones--Jimmy Jones was playing piano for her. He was her accompanist.
Uh huh.

So they wanted to get an aug--, you know, get an augmented--augmented band--so we can play arrangements and stuff. So I got guys from the University of Miami--white boys-- that could read good. I could read pretty fair, you know, I wasn't a good reader. But I could read pretty fair, you know what I mean. And we rehearsed her music and played, you know, played in the dance part. See, the Harlem Square had a big dance hall in the back and outside, I mean in the front, was a big lounge.
Uh huh.

OK, so after a while--we went on with that. So I went and asked the man--said "look here, man. We done built your--built this business up. Now we want some more money." He was paying us like $50 a week. $50 a week. Working--working six nights a week. We was only off on Mondays. And you know, well, we were making it. You know, we--wasn't none of us--we didn't have no responsibility.
Only we just had to pay for our room rent. Our room rent didn't cost that much.
Uh huh.
You know what I mean? Well, shit, man, working six nights a week and, you know, and $50 a week, I--we need some more money, you know.
Uh huh.

So he kept hemming / and hawing and he tell me "well, you know, it was worth a lot." So I said, "well, look, man. If you don't give us no more money, we going-- we going to split." And I told him we was going to leave and he said, "well, look, if you leave here, where you going to play." That's what he asked me. I said, "I don't know. I think we can play anywhere." Because we could, man because a lot of clubs wanted us to play.
Uh huh.
You know, on the beach. He said, "well I'll tell you something." He said, "if you don't play here, you're not going to play nowhere else."
Oh?

I said---"Oh?" . So I said OK. So I go and I tell--I tell--I tell the guys what he told me. So we said well, fuck it, man. Lets play up until Friday, let's play up until Thursday and if we really show them what the fuck to do. And so Friday, we didn't even show. That's when--that's the weekend. That's when everybody come to
hear us play, really.
Yeah.

Shit, man but I mean like I said, that's the same thing. Just don't take our music and say you're playing the jazz music man because you aren't playing the jazz music. You are not playing the jazz music. You're not playing the kind of blues we play. See black people music....

He'd be so busy trying to walk around here trying to act all hip and stay foolish and stuff.
That's the same thing I was trying to tell you, this is getting over man, you know trying to get around because you are black, you're the teacher. You are black so they figure
well he's my brother here. I don't have to study. I don't have to do this and I don't have to do that, because it's my brother here. I can see that he's going to let me...

That's right. I had one last week tell me that same thing. People tell me say...he was supposed to be on work study on one of those federal programs that would give minorities some money so that they can go to school and have change coming in. So the dude come in and he just wanted me to sign off so he could get his check. I said, hey man, Mister you ain't coming here. You ain't doing nothing. Well what kind of brother are you?
He's quick to call you brother.

You know, what kind of - this is my money. You ain't got nothing to do with this. All you've got to do is just sign to pay. I say hey, I'll tell you what kind of brother I am. I'm going to kick your ass. I said but I ain't going to rubberstac your bullshit. I said if you want to come in here and say that you're going to do something in the music department, you've got to come in here and put in 15 hours of work which is what the thing says. I said, there ain't nobody asking to come in here and dig no ditches. I just asked you to come in here and take these papers and get it xeroxed and take some stuff over to the mail, just little things like that. I say there ain't nobody asking to lift no weight. I said you ain't had no job man. I said where somebody

is going to have you out there digging some ditches or you've got to lift some big heavy mortar or some bricks or some cement or something like that. You ain't talking about no work man. And you don't even want to do that. You've got to be kidding. 'Well it ain't your money. The government owes me this.' I say man don't nobody owe you nothing. You've got to get out here and work. Don't a living ass owe you shit.
Yeah, that's right.
I said as long as you keep going through life thinking that somebody owes you something, you ain't never going to get nowhere.
Never get nowhere man. Always trying to get over, you know always.
....what kind of brother are you. You're going to try to run things, going through all that handshaking and all this nonsense. When I get out here, just shake my hand and just say hello.
Yeah, you've got to go through all that. I can understand.
Each cat has got a different thing, you know, start a different way and end up here or whatever. You see all that choreography. For what? What are you going to do man?
The brothers is out, ain't they? Jesus Christ, boy. It's rough. Sometimes I say man I just feel like just giving it up man. Just come on home, man, through with it, you know.
Hang that thing up on the wall.
Yeah but you've got to keep on.
You've got to keep on going. Man it's a case.
It's quite involved.
That's why jazz ain't never been dead.

Right man. You just have to you know look at those people and cuss them out just like last night man. You know nobody in the place man, nobody in this place man, me Red and Chief; so we finally, he come late anyway. He's going to come late anyway. And so okay, last night is no problem because there ain't nobody there,man. So the lady see me,man. I'm drinking Perrier and lemon, my stomach was killing me,man.
Uh huh.

See I wasn't feeling well. So we got up and played a set. I go back in the kitchen,man,and sit back there and mess around. And finally we go back and play another set . Finally at 3:30 in the morning, telling us come out there and play some more. I look at this lady, I say look here you know, that's the same reason why you all ain't got no respect for the musicians. You ain't got no respect for this man, Red Garland. You ain't got no respect for me. You ain't got no respect for him. We done sit up and played two sets in this place. Ain't nobody here. Who are we going to play to? Set up and play to you? Because you are going to pay. You could take tha little
money and go buy yourself a dress.
I thought you were going to say something else.

That's what I told her, man. I said I'm sick of your...you ain't got no God damn respect for the musicians man, you know. And I'm not playing no more. And shit, like my health comes first, man. They know I was sick, man. You know what I mean and I keep telling them, I'm not completely well man, you know. But I ain't going to go out there and complain. I'm just going along with the program man.

And the way I have to do it, if I can out of life..man, you know what I mean - shit. In this mood, I wasn't feeling well last night, boy. And they were going to have me go back up there and play some more to an empty house, to the bartender, to the tables, to the dudes standing down there, at Sonny and his friend, Now they done heard a whole set.
They hadn't even heard a whole set.

They never heard a whole set, man. You know and he's sitting down there, yeah you all play, you know. I said shit, not me, not me. I put my fiddle up and got my hat and coat, man. And I always drop Red off at his hotel. I said, look, let me tell you something, Red, I'm leaving. He said, what? I'm going to just play a little song by myself. I said, man, if you ain't ready by the time I get ready to go out this door, I'll see you later. I got in my car. I was warming it up.

That's when I saw him come out there, you know. No respect for the musicians man, you know. And that, I'm not doing any more man. I'm not because I don't need them. Them people need me. I don't need them.
That's right, that's right.
They need me, man. So that's why they opened, because they need me to come in there and play and some other musicians to come in there and play.
That's right.
So I don't need them. I didn't need them before they opened. So it's no big thing to me, you know what I mean.
See it's that attitude about your doing somebody a favor.
You aren't doing me no favor. We are doing you a favor, you see. That's the way that is.

Finally we've got this stuff turned around. Well look here, Sam. Why don't we do a rap today and then come back and get some more down so we can let you rest because it's 4:20 now, and give you a chance to warm up for the - was it Salt Peanuts?
That's a dirty name for me..

segments.title: Background: born in Jacksonville, music at home, guitar, Tampa
segments.summary: Sam gives his birth date and place, family music, his uncle's guitar and blues, the move to Tampa and playing guitar in church until a funeral ended it.

segments.title: Childhood kidney infection and hospital stay
segments.summary: He was a sickly child born with an infected kidney and spent a long time in hospital with a drainage tube.

segments.title: Hearing Oscar Pettiford's bass solo on a juke box
segments.summary: Walking in Tampa he hears a Wynonie Harris record with an Oscar Pettiford bass solo and spends his fare to hear it twice.

segments.title: Ybor City, his night-working teachers and the school dance band
segments.summary: He describes his Spanish and Cuban Ybor City neighborhood, teachers who gigged at night, and bandmaster Mr. Rodriguez's school dance band that lacked a bass.

segments.title: Buying a bass and ruining it with white paint
segments.summary: He talks his family into buying a bass on time, paints it white, ruins its sound, and mentions Clarinet Brown's youth band.

segments.title: First bass job and the first $50 pay envelope
segments.summary: Older men in a Central Avenue club hire him; he knows few standards but gets by on blues, and is stunned by $50 pay, more than his uncle earned.

segments.title: Brass Rail trio in Tampa and local resentment
segments.summary: With Ralph Dewey, Johnny Burdine and a drummer he works the Brass Rail for $125 a week, and local men resent the young stars.

segments.title: Charlie Brantley's Honey Dippers with Ray Charles
segments.summary: The best band in town copies Louis Jordan records exactly, with Ray Charles on piano singing Charles Brown and Nat Cole songs, working seven nights a week.

segments.title: Ray Charles as a young man, the trio and the Seattle offer
segments.summary: Sam recalls blind Ray Charles' independence and wildness, their trio, and why Sam declined to go with him to Seattle.

segments.title: Moving to Miami to the Entertainers Club and Frank Brown's band
segments.summary: With Johnny Burdine he moves to Miami to work with Rubin Mitchell at the Entertainers Club, where Frank Brown's big band plays; Ridley clarifies the timeline.

segments.title: Meeting the touring big bands in Tampa, Lunceford's gentlemen
segments.summary: He met the bands' buses in Tampa and admired the sharp dress of Jimmie Lunceford's men versus other bands.

segments.title: Cootie Williams' big band and 'Round Midnight
segments.summary: Cootie Williams' band with Bud Powell and Eddie Vinson knocked him out; he followed it around Florida and explains Cootie's bridge to 'Round Midnight.

segments.title: The sick baritone player and Bud Powell, Cleanhead Vinson
segments.summary: He took the ailing baritone player to a doctor, who later died, and recalls first seeing Bud Powell and Eddie Vinson's soloing.

segments.title: Louis Armstrong's band in Miami and Arvell Shaw
segments.summary: A new club opens with Louis Armstrong's orchestra; he gives Arvell Shaw a string and describes Miami nightclubs with floor shows.

segments.title: Fired from the Entertainers Club after the Tampa football trip
segments.summary: Asked about race, he instead tells how the band left for a Tampa football game and was fired.

segments.title: The bebop band at the Harlem Square
segments.summary: Hitting on owner Joe for a job, he forms a bebop sextet with Blue Mitchell, Noel Cruz, Johnny Burdine and Abe Meeks, learning from records.

segments.title: White audiences and the police shut-down at Harlem Square
segments.summary: White musicians and patrons from Miami Beach flood in, the papers write about race mixing, and the police chief clears them out.

segments.title: Backing Sarah Vaughan with Jimmy Jones
segments.summary: The club books Sarah Vaughan with Jimmy Jones, so Sam assembles an augmented band with University of Miami players.

segments.title: Demanding more than $50 a week and walking out
segments.summary: The band, paid $50 a week, asks for a raise, is threatened with being unable to play anywhere, and skips the weekend.

segments.title: Thad Jones and violinist Ray Perry sit in
segments.summary: Thad Jones loses his job by sitting in nightly, and Sam praises Ray Perry's Parker-like jazz violin and the Perry brothers.

segments.title: Blackballed along the Florida coast, deciding to leave for Jersey City
segments.summary: The group is dated to 1948, tried in Hallandale, then fired under pressure on the owner's liquor license, so Sam calls his father in Jersey City.

segments.chapter: Road bands: Hucklebuck Williams and Tiny Bradshaw
segments.title: Leaving Florida with Paul "Hucklebuck" Williams's band
segments.summary: Sam takes the first band through needing a bass player, Hucklebuck Williams's, and describes its musicians and the midget dancer.

segments.chapter: Road bands: Hucklebuck Williams and Tiny Bradshaw
segments.title: Hucklebuck dance act and the Ferguson Hotel in Indianapolis
segments.summary: Ridley asks about the Hucklebuck dancer, and they recall the band staying at the Ferguson Hotel in Indianapolis.

segments.chapter: Road bands: Hucklebuck Williams and Tiny Bradshaw
segments.title: Getting high on a gig and walking off the stand
segments.summary: A club owner gives Sam marijuana and he is too high to play, walking off the stand; the leaders suspect a heavy drug habit.

segments.chapter: Road bands: Hucklebuck Williams and Tiny Bradshaw
segments.title: Redeeming himself and the torn-up notice
segments.summary: Sam plays hard the next night, explains the reefer, and Paul tears up his notice.

segments.chapter: Road bands: Hucklebuck Williams and Tiny Bradshaw
segments.title: The bus fire on New Year's morning near Tuskegee
segments.summary: The band bus burns on the way to a Tuskegee homecoming; Sam saves his bass while the horns and clothes are lost and the school helps out.

segments.chapter: Road bands: Hucklebuck Williams and Tiny Bradshaw
segments.title: Stage show routines and Curtis Porter's back-beat story
segments.summary: The band turns to showmanship at the Howard Theatre, and Curtis Porter flees a wrong-way back beat at the Glass Bar in St. Louis.

segments.chapter: Road bands: Hucklebuck Williams and Tiny Bradshaw
segments.title: Quitting and joining Tiny Bradshaw's band through Red Prysock
segments.summary: Sam quits Hucklebuck's band and is recruited outside the Hotel Theresa by Red Prysock for Tiny Bradshaw's thirty-five-night tour.

segments.chapter: Road bands: Hucklebuck Williams and Tiny Bradshaw
segments.title: First night with Bradshaw's band, Bill Hardman and Philip Paul
segments.summary: Peck Morrison is leaving, Sam sits in at a packed gig, meets young Bill Hardman and Philip Paul, and finds the band hot.

segments.chapter: Road bands: Hucklebuck Williams and Tiny Bradshaw
segments.title: Tiny Bradshaw as a dapper bandleader
segments.summary: Bradshaw is a flashy dresser who plays only in the key of C on piano and then sings.

segments.chapter: Road bands: Hucklebuck Williams and Tiny Bradshaw
segments.title: Bradshaw's pay, $35 a night, and learning to be a professional
segments.summary: Bradshaw carries a safe in his car trunk and pays $35 a night against $22 elsewhere.

segments.chapter: Road bands: Hucklebuck Williams and Tiny Bradshaw
segments.title: Bradshaw's "three sons" and lending his Lincoln
segments.summary: The three young clean-living players are treated as sons, drive Bradshaw's Lincoln between gigs, and learn how to carry themselves.

segments.title: Back in New York, Kenny Dorham hears Sam at a session
segments.summary: After Bradshaw's death Sam plays sessions at the Paradise Club and Kenny Dorham invites him into the Jazz Prophets.

segments.title: Forming the Jazz Prophets with Dick Katz and J. R. Monterose
segments.summary: Dorham's band has Dick Katz, J. R. Monterose and Arthur Edgehill, and a weak rhythm section until Bobby Timmons is called.

segments.title: Cafe Bohemia opposite Miles Davis's quintet; Bohemia After Dark
segments.summary: Dorham's band plays against Miles's band with Red Garland, Paul Chambers and Philly Joe, which scares them; the Dorham-Miles tension and the live album.

segments.title: Why Dorham hired Dick Katz; J. R. Monterose and Edgehill
segments.summary: Ridley asks about the mixed band, and Sam says Dorham hoped it would get work, though the piano did not fit.

segments.title: First jazz gig nerves and Kenny Dorham's reckless driving
segments.summary: Sam is scared playing next to Paul Chambers, and Dorham crashes his convertible while fleeing state troopers.

segments.title: Cannonball Adderley's 1956 band with Junior Mance and Jimmy Cobb
segments.summary: Cannonball asks Sam into his band, but Junior Mance's nervous playing keeps it from gelling and the band breaks up when members drift off.

segments.title: Joining Stan Getz with Jimmy Cobb; Getz fires a pianist for applause
segments.summary: Sam and Jimmy Cobb join Getz, who is deep in drugs; in St. Louis he fires pianist John after a big ovation.

segments.title: Walking out on Getz and Mose Allison's arrival
segments.summary: Cobb confronts Getz, who cries, and sends for Mose Allison, who then stands up to him on stage.

segments.title: Getz at Storyville in Boston and Father O'Connor's girls
segments.summary: Getz returns from meeting Joe Gordon wrecked, scratches his face bloody on stage, and the priest marches out his teenage students.

segments.title: Getz's pregnant wife begs Sam to return
segments.summary: After Sam quits, Getz sends his wife to beg him to stay and then calls from South America.

segments.title: Dizzy Gillespie's small band of the late fifties
segments.summary: Sam describes Dizzy's unrecorded small band with Sonny Stitt, Wynton Kelly, Jimmy Cobb and Candido.

segments.title: Pittsburgh engagement with Miles and Coltrane listening
segments.summary: In snowy Pittsburgh crowds line up for Dizzy's band while Miles and Coltrane watch from the audience.

segments.title: Sonny Stitt pressures Dizzy and Dizzy bows to him
segments.summary: Stitt's long solo draws huge applause, so Dizzy answers with a long solo and takes his bow to Stitt.

segments.title: Dizzy's dislike of pressure, Cheraw drunkenness and pot on the plane
segments.summary: Sam recalls Dizzy playing congas, a drunken night in his hometown Cheraw, and passing his pot pipe on planes.

segments.title: Nervous breakdown, quitting Dizzy and the club owner at knifepoint
segments.summary: Sam's stomach trouble is tied by doctors to the band; in Miami Beach Dizzy pulls a switchblade on a complaining club owner.

segments.title: Joining Thelonious Monk: no rehearsals
segments.summary: Monk calls Sam, refuses to rehearse, and Charlie Rouse says to keep bugging him; Monk's extra bars are hard.

segments.title: Arthur Taylor's car wreck in New Jersey and Coltrane's rescue
segments.summary: Arthur Taylor crashes his new car after a New Jersey gig and Coltrane leaves the Cafe Bohemia stand to drive them home.

segments.title: Leaving Monk in California; Cannonball restarts his band
segments.summary: Sam dates the wreck to about 1960 and quits Monk's band in Los Angeles after Cannonball phones him.

segments.title: Live recording at the Jazz Workshop and the hit 'This Here'
segments.summary: The new Cannonball band with Bobby Timmons and Louis Hayes records live in San Francisco, and Timmons's tune becomes a hit.

segments.title: Commercial records bother Sam; Cannonball's intelligence
segments.summary: Sam says the hit records troubled him given how intelligent and versatile Cannonball was.

segments.title: Nat Adderley's cornet and his influence on the band
segments.summary: Nat had great range but never practiced and did not know changes.

segments.title: Commercial songs, Nancy Wilson tours and billing
segments.summary: Sam hated songs like Work Song and Jive Samba; the Nancy Wilson record turned the billing to Nancy Wilson and friends.

segments.title: The sextet with Charles Lloyd and Zawinul at its best
segments.summary: At a Columbus concert Sam recalls the powerful sextet rhythm section of Zawinul, himself and Louis Hayes.

segments.title: Telling the band he hated the commercial music, Nat's challenge
segments.summary: Sam tells the Columbus audience how he felt, wants to be a creative musician, and Nat invites him to fight.

segments.title: Oscar Peterson's phone call and leaving Cannonball with Louis Hayes
segments.summary: Peterson phones Sam in Seattle at 5 a.m. to replace Ray Brown, Louis Hayes is also asked, and Sam takes double the pay.

segments.title: Rehearsing in Canada and learning Peterson's difficult trio parts
segments.summary: Sam flies to Canada to rehearse, tours small colleges, and struggles with the written unison parts but takes it as a challenge.

segments.title: Five and a half years with Peterson and playing 3/4 loose
segments.summary: The trio with Sam and Louis Hayes won attention, and their loose way of playing 3/4 time amazed Peterson and freed him.

segments.title: Poll wins, constant travel and quitting at the Plaza Nine
segments.summary: Sam wins awards but tires of airports, sees a three-week Plaza Nine booking, and decides to leave the trio.

segments.title: Freelancing in New York, Wynton Kelly at Mikell's and Toronto
segments.summary: Back in New York Sam plays duo with Wynton Kelly at Mikell's and encourages him to take a Toronto job.

segments.title: Angry Squire and Boomer's, playing in the club window
segments.summary: With Cedar Walton and Billy Higgins at the Angry Squire, and with Bobby Timmons at Boomer's, they are made to play in windows until bandstands are built.

segments.title: Cedar Walton and the great Messengers and Horace Silver bands
segments.summary: Sam knew Walton from the 125 Club, and he and Ridley praise Blakey's sextet and Silver's band.

segments.title: The Cannonball sextet with Yusef Lateef
segments.summary: Yusef Lateef's big tone, flute and oboe, and his compositions made the sextet popular, including at the Comblain-la-Tour festival.

segments.title: Charles Lloyd replaces Yusef, Nat's dislike of him
segments.summary: Lloyd brings freer music and a strong audience reaction at the Apollo, but Nat hated him and his flute was out of tune.

segments.title: Recording Fiddler on the Roof on short notice
segments.summary: The record company drops the Fiddler on the Roof score, rehearsed at Pep's in Philadelphia, but the album sold only modestly.

segments.title: Here Comes Charlie, the live album, and why they kept a quintet
segments.summary: Sam objects to the tired music for Here Comes Charlie, a live album with Lloyd sells poorly, and the band drops the sextet.

segments.title: The Japanese singer's tour offer to the Walton-Higgins trio
segments.summary: Sam, Cedar Walton and Billy Higgins are invited to Japan by a pop singer, and record there with Sadao Watanabe and Hisao Suzuki.

segments.title: Making the Sam Jones String Quartet album for East Wind
segments.summary: He insists on a string quartet, Cedar writes four arrangements, and they record in Tokyo; later Japan tours continue.

segments.title: Forming the 12-piece band and falling ill
segments.summary: Sam builds a twelve-piece band, gets bookings at the Vanguard and Gulliver's and a contract, then takes sick.

segments.title: Ending the first session; second session's plan
segments.summary: Ridley ends the first day's interview, and at the next session proposes specific conceptual questions.

segments.title: Is jazz an art form: America's classical music
segments.summary: Sam says jazz is America's classical music and criticizes fusion and radio stations like WRVR.

segments.title: Defining jazz: blues, funerals and not only New Orleans
segments.summary: Sam defines jazz as music from within yourself and tells of Tampa funeral marches and the return jam.

segments.title: Fusion versus jazz and Weather Report's claim
segments.summary: Ridley argues the fusion side; Sam says classical jazz is its own history and denies Weather Report's claims.

segments.title: The word bebop
segments.summary: Sam says bebop came from musicians' scat syllables in the 1940s and he does not know of it as a label.

segments.title: Record companies, big signing money, and musicians who went commercial
segments.summary: Sam argues companies push musicians into commercial music, naming Dexter Gordon, Sonny Rollins, Donald Byrd and Miles.

segments.title: What defines each jazz style: Bird's influence and others following
segments.summary: Ridley asks whether period styles define jazz; Sam says a unique voice like Bird's draws everyone in, and compares it to disco.

segments.title: The layman and the back beat in freedom music
segments.summary: Sam says the working listener lost the beat with freedom music, and Ridley argues fusion revives it.

segments.title: Bland fusion melodies and Cedar Walton's too-musical records
segments.summary: Sam says fusion melodies repeat without thought and only Cedar Walton puts music in it, which is why it won't sell.

segments.title: Hubbard, Turrentine and Benson: hit-making versus expressing feelings
segments.summary: Sam judges Freddie Hubbard, Stanley Turrentine and George Benson by whether they aim for hits.

segments.title: Individuals versus group names in rock-era marketing
segments.summary: Ridley asks, with George Russell's view, whether group emphasis replaced individuality.

segments.title: Commercial groups of old: Amos Milburn's honkers at the Howard Theatre
segments.summary: With Hucklebuck Williams at the Howard, Milburn's honking showmen beat their written book, so Paul had them close the books and dance.

segments.title: Managers and record men fleecing vocal groups like the Clovers
segments.summary: Sam says the same story repeats; the Clovers were paid $250 a week while their manager held the money, and Ridley saw the same.

segments.title: Is jazz ever dead; disc jockeys and jazz teaching in schools
segments.summary: Sam says jazz has never died, blames uninformed disc jockeys, and welcomes jazz musicians teaching in schools.

segments.chapter: Young players, Coltrane and the avant-garde
segments.title: Young black musicians losing interest; the all-black band problem
segments.summary: Sam is bothered that black players skip rehearsal while white players show up, and says Thad Jones faced the same.

segments.chapter: Young players, Coltrane and the avant-garde
segments.title: Hidden young talent around the country and lack of respect
segments.summary: Ridley describes talent in Gary and New Orleans, and both bemoan young players without pride or respect.

segments.chapter: Young players, Coltrane and the avant-garde
segments.title: New Orleans musical families, New York backbiting and Lockjaw's jam sessions
segments.summary: Sam says New Orleans players learn from fathers, and recalls Eddie Lockjaw Davis publicly correcting weak players as a lesson.

segments.chapter: Young players, Coltrane and the avant-garde
segments.title: The Freedom School and Coltrane letting players on stage
segments.summary: They discuss how Coltrane let weak players come up and tell their stories.

segments.chapter: Young players, Coltrane and the avant-garde
segments.title: Coltrane shows his chord chart at home
segments.summary: Sam and Yusef Lateef visit Coltrane, who explains his chart of chords around each key.

segments.chapter: Young players, Coltrane and the avant-garde
segments.title: Coltrane knew what he was doing; his practicing
segments.summary: Ridley and Sam say avant-garde players missed Coltrane's method, which belongs in schools, and he practiced constantly.

segments.chapter: Young players, Coltrane and the avant-garde
segments.title: Avant-garde players who missed the point, Sunny Murray and the cymbal
segments.summary: Ridley tells of a saxophonist standing silent at the Half Note and Sunny Murray's long wait to hit the cymbal.

segments.chapter: Young players, Coltrane and the avant-garde
segments.title: The layman, the back beat and a freedom radio program
segments.summary: The working listener just wants the beat; Sam switches off a WBGO announcer who plays only freedom music.

segments.chapter: Race, critics and the big bands
segments.title: Was there a conspiracy to push the avant-garde
segments.summary: Ridley asks about critics promoting freedom music; Sam says there were no black writers and the press called the old records alike.

segments.chapter: Race, critics and the big bands
segments.title: White hopes and Miles's band: making room for white stars
segments.summary: Sam believes writers had to move black bands aside to make room for Mulligan, Chet Baker and Getz, and says Miles's band blocked it.

segments.chapter: Race, critics and the big bands
segments.title: Critic bias in reviews, Paul Whiteman and Benny Goodman
segments.summary: Ridley notes critics qualify praise of black artists, and they trace it from James Reese Europe and Whiteman to Goodman.

segments.chapter: Race, critics and the big bands
segments.title: Jimmy Lunceford, Sy Oliver and black arrangers behind white bands
segments.summary: Sam calls Lunceford the greatest band; they discuss white bands taking black arrangements and Eldridge, Shavers, Charlie Barnet.

segments.chapter: Race, critics and the big bands
segments.title: The big bands that passed through Florida, Snookum Russell and Roy Haynes
segments.summary: Sam recalls the many big bands, Carolina Cottonpickers and Louis Russell's band where he met Ray Brown and Roy Haynes.

segments.chapter: Race, critics and the big bands
segments.title: Meeting every band at the bus as a kid in Florida
segments.summary: Sam says he met all the bands as a kid, so he knew everyone when he reached New York, including Oscar Pettiford.

segments.chapter: Race, critics and the big bands
segments.title: Family bands: the Pettifords and Slide Hampton's band
segments.summary: Sam did not hear the Pettiford family band but often heard Slide Hampton's family band stuck in Florida.

segments.chapter: Race, critics and the big bands
segments.title: Buddy Johnson's commercial dance band
segments.summary: Sam describes Buddy Johnson's good book and his singers.

segments.chapter: Race, critics and the big bands
segments.title: Jay McShann's raggedy band with Bird and patio dances at home
segments.summary: Sam wanted to hear McShann's band with Parker, Ramey and Gus Johnson, and remembers outdoor patio dances.

segments.title: Polls are rigged by money, bass poll winners
segments.summary: Sam says polls can be won by money and names bassists like Niels-Henning Orsted Pedersen and George Mraz overlooked.

segments.title: Can you poll artists: Bach and Beethoven
segments.summary: Ridley argues that comparing individual artists in polls makes no sense.

segments.title: Stylists versus players: Hawkins, Young, Miles and Dizzy
segments.summary: Sam separates stylists like Lester Young and Miles from fine players like Chu Berry and Dizzy.

segments.title: Leonard Feather's origin of the jazz polls
segments.summary: Ridley relays that Feather started the polls to get magazines to cover black artists, and Sam recalls poll orchestras.

segments.title: Winning polls with a check and what winners owe listeners
segments.summary: Sam says anyone with money can win a poll, and poll winners are judged by listeners.

segments.title: Not Ray Brown: Sam's own style with Peterson and polls
segments.summary: Sam told writers he was no Ray Brown, and his style helped the trio win its first group poll.

segments.title: Overlooked bassists, Niels-Henning Orsted Pedersen and admitting influences
segments.summary: Sam praises George Duvivier and the young Niels Orsted Pedersen, who credits Chambers, Jones and Brown, and names his own influences.

segments.title: Why black influence goes unadmitted, Getz and Lester Young
segments.summary: Sam and Ridley say egos and race keep players like Getz from crediting black influences.

segments.title: Union 802 hiring floor and prejudice in music
segments.summary: Sam says only white names are called for gigs on the union floor and that prejudice exists everywhere.

segments.title: Jazz in European caves versus concert halls
segments.summary: Sam is angered that black players accept playing in dumps in Europe and a writer saying jazz belongs in smoky joints.

segments.title: Expatriates in Europe: Benny Bailey and rising nationalism
segments.summary: They discuss players living in Europe, Griffin and Farmer, Benny Bailey planning to return, and French attitudes.

segments.title: Refusing Europe unless paid $1,500 a week
segments.summary: After a dangerous smoky cave, Sam says he will not go back to Europe except for $1,500 plus hotel.

segments.title: Standing up for the art, not just the money
segments.summary: Sam and Ridley say musicians must stand up for rights and keep the art alive before others claim it.

segments.title: Chuck Mangione labelled jazz; dinners at his family's house
segments.summary: Sam objects to Italian folk songs being labelled jazz and recalls dinners at Mangione's family home in Rochester.

segments.title: What happened to the 8-bar blues and minor keys
segments.summary: Sam asks why players no longer use 8-bar blues and minors, which express real feeling.

segments.title: Jazz education and students expecting favors
segments.summary: Ridley says jazz programs teach cliches and Sam says black students expect favors as brothers.

segments.title: Ridley's work-study student and 'what kind of brother'
segments.summary: Ridley tells of a student who wanted his work-study check signed without working.

segments.title: Walking out on a club that shows no respect, with Red Garland
segments.summary: Sam describes a nearly empty club where the owner demanded more sets, and says musicians are doing the club a favor.

segments.title: Closing the session
segments.summary: Ridley ends the session so Sam can rest before his gig.
